definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of the embodied self: it cannot be an object of thought (2.25, with 'unmanifest' and 'unchangeable').

literal: non-dharma, what is contrary to dharma

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument, the disorder that overpowers a family once its family dharmas perish, leading to the corruption of its women and varṇa-mixture (1.40–41).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.47: one's right or proper claim, which extends to action alone and never to its fruits.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In the compound adhyātma-cetas (3.30): the mind directed to the self, with which one resigns all actions to Kṛṣṇa; commentators gloss it variously.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The sense of 'I' by which one deluded thinks 'I am the doer' while actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti (3.27); the one of steady wisdom is without it (nirahaṃkāra, 2.71).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of the embodied self: unborn, eternal, everlasting, primeval (2.20); knowing it as unborn one sees that it neither slays nor is slain (2.21).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Inaction, to which one should not be attached (2.47); action is better than inaction, and without action even the body cannot be maintained (3.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 3.15 the imperishable from which brahman arises (in the chain: action from brahman, brahman from the imperishable); its identification is disputed among commentators.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The goal for which the steadfast person, unmoved by the contacts of the senses and the same in pleasure and pain, is fit (2.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of the sense-contacts that give cold and heat, pleasure and pain: they come and go and are impermanent, so are to be endured (2.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In the cycle of 3.14: beings come from food, food from rain, rain from sacrifice.

literal: immeasurable, not an object of the means of knowledge

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of the eternal embodied one whose bodies have an end (2.18).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The manner of action taught in chapter 3: the karma-yogin acts unattached (3.7); one should always perform the action to be done unattached, thereby reaching the highest (3.19); the wise act unattached for the holding together of the world (3.25).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.16: that of which there is no coming to be (bhāva); what exactly is meant is disputed among commentators.

literal: one who has drawn [his bow], an aggressor

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's description of the Kauravas as aggressors, whose killing he says would still bring sin (1.36).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The self: the one of steady wisdom is content in the self by the self (2.55); for one who delights in the self alone there is nothing to be done (3.17); what is beyond the understanding is to be known, and the self steadied by the self (3.42–43). In these chapters it is more often referred to as 'the embodied one' (dehin, śarīrin).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The condition of the person who delights in, is satisfied in and content in the self alone, for whom nothing remains to be done and who depends on no being for any purpose (3.17–18).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of the embodied self (2.25), and of the beginning and end of beings, whose middle only is manifest (2.28).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of that by which all this is pervaded, which no one can destroy (2.17), and of the self known as indestructible and unborn (2.21).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What the unyoked lack; without it there is no peace (2.66). Commentators gloss it as steady contemplation, dwelling on the self, or conviction.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Beings, whose beginning and end are unmanifest and middle manifest (2.28), and who arise from food (3.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What one attains who abides in the brahmic state even at the time of death (2.72); first use of the term in the text.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.72 in the compounds brāhmī sthiti and brahmanirvāṇa (the state and goal of the one of steady wisdom). In 3.15 'brahma' arises from the imperishable and is the source of action, and the 'all-pervading brahman' is established in sacrifice; commentators take brahma in 3.15 as the Veda or as prakṛti.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.46 the 'knowing brāhmaṇa', for whom all the Vedas are of as much use as a well amid a flood.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The state of the one of steady wisdom described in 2.55–71; having attained it one is not bewildered, and abiding in it even at death one attains brahma-nirvāṇa (2.72).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Understanding: the teaching given 'in sāṃkhya' and now 'in yoga' (2.39); single and resolute in the discipline, many-branched in the irresolute (2.41); to be taken as refuge (2.49); destroyed at the end of the chain from anger (2.63), steadied in serenity (2.65); higher than the mind and lower than 'he' (3.42); one of the seats of desire (3.40). Arjuna asks why, if it is superior to action, he is urged to act (3.1).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The discipline of action yoked with understanding: action is far inferior to it (2.49); yoked with it one casts off good and evil deeds (2.50) and the wise, abandoning the fruit of action, are freed from the bondage of birth (2.51); introduced as the 'yoga' form of the teaching at 2.39.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What the wise should not cause in the ignorant who are attached to action (3.26; cf. 3.29 'should not unsettle').

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The self as embodied: it passes through childhood, youth, old age and into another body (2.13), casts off worn-out bodies like clothes (2.22), is eternally unslayable in every body (2.30); also called śarīrin, whose bodies have an end (2.18). Desire deludes the embodied one by covering knowledge (3.40).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The gods, nourished by sacrifice, who in turn nourish beings and give them desired enjoyments (3.11–12).

literal: what upholds; duty, right order, law

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Used of: Kurukṣetra as 'the field of dharma' (1.1); the eternal family dharmas whose loss lets adharma prevail (1.40); the matter on which Arjuna's mind is bewildered (2.7); one's own dharma, for a kṣatriya a battle accordant with dharma (2.31, 2.33, 3.35); and the teaching of buddhi-yoga itself, of which even a little saves from great fear (2.40).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The steadfast one, who is not bewildered by the passage to another body (2.13) and, unmoved by pleasure and pain, is fit for immortality (2.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: With rāga: aversion, from which the senses of the self-governed are free (2.64); attraction and aversion lie in the object of each sense and are one's waylayers (3.34).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The qualities born of prakṛti: they make everyone act helplessly (3.5); actions are done by them while the deluded thinks 'I am the doer' (3.27); the knower sees 'guṇas move among guṇas' (3.28). The Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain; Arjuna is told to be free of them (2.45). Desire is born of the guṇa rajas (3.37).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The venerable elders and teachers (Bhīṣma, Droṇa) whom Arjuna would rather live on alms than kill (2.5).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The senses: to be withdrawn from their objects like a tortoise's limbs (2.58); turbulent, they carry off the mind even of the striving (2.60); to be restrained (2.61, 2.68, 3.41); high, but lower than the mind (3.42); one of the seats of desire (3.40). Organs of action are karmendriya (3.6–7).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The objects from which the senses are to be withdrawn (2.58, 2.68), on which the hypocrite dwells in mind (3.6), and in which attraction and aversion are set (3.34).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The bondage from which the wise, yoked with understanding and abandoning the fruit of action, are freed (2.51).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The dharmas of the birth-group which, with the family dharmas, Arjuna says are uprooted by the faults of family-destroyers (1.43).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Knowledge, covered by desire the constant enemy of the knower (3.38–40); desire is the destroyer of knowledge and discernment (jñāna-vijñāna, 3.41); those who reject the teaching are deluded in all knowledge (3.32).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The commitment (niṣṭhā) of the sāṃkhyas, one of the two declared by Kṛṣṇa of old (3.3).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Desire: the ritual-minded are 'desire-souled' (2.43); the one of steady wisdom gives up all desires that enter the mind (2.55, 2.71) and is entered by desires like the ocean without being moved (2.70); desire is born of attachment and gives rise to anger (2.62); named with anger as the enemy born of rajas that covers knowledge, seated in the senses, mind and understanding, to be slain (3.37–43).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Action: one's right is to action, not to its fruits (2.47); no one remains a moment without action (3.5); allotted action is better than inaction (3.8); action binds except when done for sacrifice (3.9); sacrifice arises from action and action from brahman (3.14–15); by action Janaka and others reached perfection (3.20). Arjuna asks why he is urged to action if understanding is superior (3.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The bondage of action which one yoked with the understanding of yoga casts off (2.39); the world is 'bound by action' (karma-bandhana) except action for sacrifice (3.9).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The commitment of the yogins, one of the two declared by Kṛṣṇa of old (3.3); undertaken with the organs of action by one who controls the senses with the mind and is unattached (3.7).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The fruit of action, to which one has no right and which should not be one's motive (2.47); those whose motive is the fruit are wretched (2.49); the wise abandon the fruit born of action (2.51); the ritual-minded's speech offers birth as the fruit of action (2.43).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The organs of action: restraining them while the mind dwells on objects is hypocrisy (3.6); with them, senses controlled by the mind, one undertakes karma-yoga (3.7).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The fault (kārpaṇya-doṣa) by which Arjuna says his very nature is struck when he asks for instruction (2.7).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 3.27: the ego-deluded thinks 'I am the doer' (kartā aham) while actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The dejection that has come upon Arjuna at the critical moment, not practised by the noble, not leading to heaven, bringing disgrace (2.2).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.50 yoga is defined as 'skill in actions' (karmasu kauśalam).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The unmanliness to which Arjuna is told not to yield, with 'petty weakness of heart' (hṛdaya-daurbalya) (2.3).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Anger: arises from desire and gives rise to delusion (2.62–63); the sage of steady thought is free from it (2.56); named with desire as the enemy born of rajas (3.37).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The pity by which Arjuna is overcome on seeing his kin (1.28, 2.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: For a kṣatriya there is nothing better than a battle accordant with dharma (2.31); happy the kṣatriyas who get such a battle, a door to heaven (2.32).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The destruction of a family, whose fault Arjuna says the greedy Kauravas do not see but he does (1.38–39); it destroys the family dharmas (1.40).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The eternal dharmas of a family, which perish when the family is destroyed, leading to adharma, varṇa-mixture and hell (1.40, 1.43–44).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Greed: Arjuna says the Kauravas' minds are struck by it (1.38) and that his own side is ready to kill from greed for kingship (1.45).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The holding together of the world, with a view to which one should act (3.20) and the wise act unattached (3.25), since people follow the standard the best person sets (3.21).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The mind: it seems to whirl in Arjuna's despondency (1.30); desires that enter it are to be given up (2.55); the turbulent senses carry it off (2.60, 2.67); dwelling in it on objects while restraining the organs of action is hypocrisy (3.6); higher than the senses and lower than the understanding (3.42); one of the seats of desire (3.40).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Kṛṣṇa's teaching (me matam), which those who follow with faith are released from actions and those who cavil at are lost (3.31–32).

literal: contact of the mātrās (senses with their objects)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The sense-contacts that give cold and heat, pleasure and pain, come and go, impermanent, to be endured (2.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One who restrains the organs of action but sits dwelling in mind on sense-objects (3.6).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Delusion: the thicket of delusion (moha-kalila) understanding must cross (2.52); saṃmoha arises from anger and leads to loss of memory (2.63); the one in the brahmic state is not bewildered (2.72); Arjuna says Kṛṣṇa's mixed speech bewilders his understanding (3.2).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The sage of steady thought (2.56), awake in what is night for all beings (2.69).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Not attained by not undertaking actions (3.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument: varṇa-mixture leads family-destroyers and the family to hell (1.42); those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell in hell for an indefinite time, as 'we have heard' (1.44).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 3.33: beings follow their nature — 'what will restraint accomplish?'

literal: free from the pairs of opposites

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One of the qualities Arjuna is told to have when free of the three guṇas (2.45).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Without the sense of 'mine': the one who attains peace (2.71); Arjuna is to fight nirmama (3.30).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The indifference to what is to be heard and what has been heard reached when understanding crosses the thicket of delusion (2.52).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The twofold commitment declared by Kṛṣṇa of old: by the yoga of knowledge for the sāṃkhyas and by the yoga of action for the yogins (3.3).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What Arjuna is told to be, the Vedas having the three guṇas as their domain (2.45).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of the embodied self (2.18, 2.20, 2.24); in 2.26 the contrary hypothesis that it is 'constantly' born and dying.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The action Arjuna is told to perform, action being better than inaction (3.8); commentators take niyata as 'prescribed/obligatory'.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The wise, who grieve neither for the dead nor for the living (2.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Sin: Arjuna fears it would cling to them for killing kin (1.36, 1.39, 1.45); Kṛṣṇa says refusing the dharmic battle incurs it (2.33) while fighting with equanimity does not (2.38); those who cook only for themselves eat sin (agha, 3.13); Arjuna asks what drives a person to sin against his will (3.36).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Another's dharma, even well performed, is worse than one's own deficient dharma and brings danger (3.35).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 1.42: the ancestors fall when deprived of the rites of rice-ball and water offerings (piṇḍa-udaka-kriyā).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The ancestors, who fall when deprived of the rice-ball and water offerings because of varṇa-mixture (1.42).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The creator who in the beginning created beings together with sacrifice and told them to prosper by it (3.10).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Wisdom that is 'firmly established' in one who is unattached and withdraws and masters the senses (2.57, 2.58, 2.61, 2.68); the mind that follows the roving senses carries it off (2.67).

literal: nature, primal matter; one's own nature

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Prakṛti, whose guṇas make everyone act (3.5, 3.27, 3.29); also one's own nature, which even the person of knowledge follows (3.33).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The serenity attained by the self-governed who move among objects with senses free of attraction and aversion; in it all sorrows end and understanding becomes steady (2.64–65).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The adverse result which is not found in the yoga of understanding (2.40).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Passion, from which the sage of steady thought is free (2.56); with aversion, lies in wait in the objects of the senses (2.64, 3.34).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The guṇa from which desire and anger arise (3.37).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The inner taste for sense-objects that remains when one abstains from them and turns away only on seeing the highest (2.59).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In which the resolute understanding of the ritual-minded is not established (2.44); in which understanding must stand immovable for one to attain yoga (2.53); the one of steady wisdom is 'established in samādhi' (2.54). Commentators gloss the word variously in these verses.

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Sameness in success and failure, which 'is called yoga' (2.48); making pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same (2.38); the steadfast is the same in pain and pleasure (2.15).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The way in which the understanding of 2.11–38 was declared, contrasted with 'yoga' (2.39); the sāṃkhyas are those whose commitment is the yoga of knowledge (3.3). The chunk does not relate the term to a school.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Mere renunciation (saṃnyasana) does not bring perfection (3.4); Arjuna is to 'lay down' (saṃnyasya) all actions in Kṛṣṇa (3.30).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The perfection Janaka and others reached by action (3.20).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The self-restrained, awake in what is night for all beings (2.69).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Attachment: not to inaction (2.47); to be abandoned in action (2.48, 3.9); arises from dwelling on objects and gives rise to desire (2.62); the ignorant are attached to action and to the actions of the guṇas (3.26, 3.29); the knower is not attached (3.28).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Peace, not possible without contemplation (2.66); attained by one whom desires enter like waters the ocean, and by one who abandons all desires, without 'mine' and 'I' (2.70–71).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Said of the embodied self (2.24) and of brahman established in sacrifice (3.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.16: that of which there is no ceasing to be (abhāva); what exactly is meant is disputed among commentators.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.45 'nitya-sattva-stha' (ever abiding in sattva / in what is real); commentators divide on the sense.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Success, to be regarded the same as failure (2.48); perfection, not reached by mere renunciation (3.4).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple and asks to be instructed (2.7); Duryodhana calls Dhṛṣṭadyumna Droṇa's disciple (1.3).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Memory, confused by delusion; its loss destroys understanding (2.63).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's grief, which overwhelms him (1.47) and dries up his senses (2.8); Kṛṣṇa's teaching is that the self is not to be grieved for (2.11, 2.25–27, 2.30).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who follow Kṛṣṇa's teaching with faith and without cavilling are released from actions (3.31).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: What Arjuna cannot see in killing kin (1.31) and asks to be told decisively (2.7, 3.2); the 'highest good' attained by mutual nourishment of gods and humans through sacrifice (3.11).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 2.53 understanding 'perplexed by śruti' (by what has been heard / by scriptural statements) must become steady in samādhi; cf. 2.52 'what is to be heard and what has been heard'.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Synonym of sthitaprajña in Arjuna's question (2.54); the sage whose mind is unshaken by sorrow and pleasure and free of passion, fear and anger (2.56).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The person described in 2.55–72: gives up all desires that enter the mind, content in the self by the self (2.55); his wisdom is firmly established when he is unattached, withdraws the senses and masters them (2.57–68); his state is the brāhmī sthiti (2.72).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One's own dharma: for Arjuna the kṣatriya's dharmic battle (2.31, 2.33); better even when deficient than another's dharma well performed (3.35).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Heaven: Arjuna's faintness does not lead to it (2.2); a dharmic battle is its open door (2.32) and the slain warrior attains it (2.37); the ritual-minded are intent on it (2.43).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who have seen the final truth about the real and the unreal (2.16).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The knower of the truth about the division of guṇas and actions, who is not attached (3.28).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Enduring (titikṣasva) the impermanent sense-contacts that give cold and heat, pleasure and pain (2.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The domain of the Vedas (traiguṇya-viṣayāḥ vedāḥ, 2.45).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The social orders whose mixture (varṇa-saṅkara) Arjuna fears (1.41).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument, the mixture of social orders that arises when the family's women are corrupted after adharma prevails, leading to hell and the ancestors' fall (1.41–43); Kṛṣṇa says he would be the maker of saṅkara if he did not act (3.24).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The Vedas, whose statements the undiscerning delight in (2.42), which have the three guṇas as their domain (2.45), and which are of as much use to the knowing brāhmaṇa as a well amid a flood (2.46).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who delight in vedavāda say 'there is nothing else' and proclaim flowery speech offering heaven, power and rebirth as fruit of works (2.42–43).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: With jñāna, what desire destroys (3.41); commentators differ on the distinction.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's despondency on seeing his kin (1.28, 2.1, 2.10).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The sense-objects: they turn away from one who abstains, though the taste remains (2.59); dwelling on them breeds attachment (2.62); the self-governed move among them with mastered senses (2.64).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Resolute understanding, which is single (2.41) and is not established in samādhi in those attached to enjoyment and power (2.44).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Sacrifice: action done for its sake does not bind (3.9); beings were created with it by Prajāpati, it nourishes the gods who nourish beings (3.10–12); eating its remains frees from faults (3.13); it arises from action and brings rain (3.14); brahman is established in it (3.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The remains of sacrifice, eating which the good are freed from all faults (3.13).

Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In these chapters: the way in which the understanding is now taught, contrasted with sāṃkhya (2.39); 'sameness is called yoga' (2.48); 'yoga is skill in actions' (2.50); what one attains when understanding stands steady in samādhi (2.53).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna is told to be free of concern for acquiring and keeping (niryogakṣema) (2.45).
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In 3.3 the yogins are those whose commitment is the yoga of action.
Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The yoked one who, restraining the senses, sits intent on Kṛṣṇa (2.61); the unyoked has neither understanding nor contemplation (2.66); the wise act yoked (3.26).
